extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of the history of advertising; historians and general readers interested in historical print advertisements and handbills
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and analysing features, conventions, and persuasive devices used in historical handbills, posters, and small printed advertisements (theatrical bills, showmen's handbills, school prospectuses, burial-society notices, trade cards, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of Performance each Day.
rubrics_metrics.description: Theatrical bills explicitly state that the performance changes daily and give the day's programme (title, subtitle, cast, roles, concluding scenes and subsequent entertainments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the title (often with a subtitle), cast list with role assignments, a note of the concluding scene(s) (e.g., 'The Piece concludes with the Death of Orsina, and the Appearance of the ACCUSING SPIRIT'), and the follow-on entertainment (e.g., pantomime, harlequinade). Also list ticket prices (Boxes, Pit, Gallery) and any special attractions or new features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote spectacle: 'New Scenery, Tricks, Dresses, and Decorations' / 'A SPLENDID PANORAMA'.
rubrics_metrics.description: Entertainment advertisements emphasise visual and technical spectacle—new scenery, stage tricks, costumes, panoramas, and displays by 'first artists'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight novel visual elements and the names/roles of performers to promise a spectacular experience; use superlatives and words indicating novelty or ‘first’ artists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bilingual / multilingual presentation (keep languages separate).
rubrics_metrics.description: Some bills are printed in two languages, often maintaining separate columns or distinct phrasing for each language (example: English and French columns kept separate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing multilingual audiences, present parallel translations clearly; include lingua-framing devices (e.g., Latin or patriotic slogans) to appeal across readerships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of patriotic/authoritative inscriptions (e.g., 'Vivat Rex').
rubrics_metrics.description: Showmen and advertisers sometimes include Latin/formal inscriptions and royal formulas to lend authority or patriotic cachet (example: the showman uses 'Vivat Rex' under his French).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add short authoritative or patriotic tags to signal official favour, dignity, or respectable standing; these can reassure or attract certain audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism and marvellous storytelling to excite a 'sensation'.
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverts for curiosities and shows deploy marvellous, extravagant stories (e.g., 'Surpassijtg all Prodigies', 'strange Births') that may outrage decency and probability to excite public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sensational language and improbable detail to attract crowds—but expect critics to note when decency or probability is outraged; sensationalism is effective for popular curiosity attractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal challenge/duel as promotional device (public dare).
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals advertise personal challenges or duels (e.g., one performer daring another to meet on stage) with specific time, place, and an explicit promise that action will decide a controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State exact venue and times (doors opening hours, when performers mount), frame the encounter as decisive spectacle, and promise audience 'satisfaction'—use bravado to draw spectators.

rubrics_metrics.name: School prospectus: curriculum, ages, languages, fees, and outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational advertisements/prospectuses list the subjects taught (works of all sorts, dancing, music, singing, writing, accounts, Latin/French/Greek/Hebrew/Italian/Spanish), age ranges, duration (e.g., 'Gentlewomen of eight or nine Years old... may be instructed in a Year or two'), fees (e.g., '£20 per Annum'), and promises about competency/outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give clear, itemised lists of instruction areas, expected timelines for attainment, optional subjects, fee structure, and any conditional surcharge for superior improvement; name the proprietor/undertaker and where to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbered list of concrete benefits and comparative claims (product claims).
rubrics_metrics.description: Product advertisements (e.g., Beetham's washing mill) enumerate benefits with numbered points (1, 2, 3, 4) describing superiority, efficiency, cost-savings, and comparative performance (e.g., 'It renders the linen whiter...', 'It will wash more in one hour than ten women').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear numbered claims to make benefits digestible; include measurable comparisons, claimed savings, and an explanation of economic payback (e.g., 'price ... is very soon cleared by what it saves').

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration times and availability (show when product may be seen).
rubrics_metrics.description: Ads often give times for public demonstration or viewing (e.g., 'This invaluable invention may be seen from Eleven until Two every day').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify demonstration/viewing hours so potential buyers can inspect the product; combine with venue/address information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit price lists and variants (models/pricing).
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements present prices for different sizes/models (e.g., prices for mills that wash different numbers of shirts; price for wringer), often line-by-line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List product variants clearly with corresponding prices so customers can select by capacity or feature set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to social proof and endorsements ('Several hundreds ... allow it to excel').
rubrics_metrics.description: Ads use testimonials, general claims of many satisfied customers, or elite attention to validate a product's utility or reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include counts, named patrons, or claims of broad adoption when available; invoke royal or noble attention where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal patent / exclusivity claim as a selling point.
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising cites royal patents or granted exclusivity (e.g., 'the King grants his royal patent to the Artist') to assert protection from imitation and a special status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention patents or official grants to signify uniqueness and legal protection; explain the term/extent (e.g., 'until twice seven seasons... no man should imitate').

rubrics_metrics.name: Tombstone / memorial inscription used as business advertisement.
rubrics_metrics.description: Tradespeople sometimes place business addresses or notices on memorial stones (example: 'Sacred to the Memory of JOHN ROBERTS ... N.B. — The business carried on by the Widow at No. 1, Freshfield place').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use burial memorials or durable inscriptions to advertise services adjacent to the memorial text; though sometimes considered tasteless, it directly links trade to trade-mark context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burial society advertisement components (membership model and service specification).
rubrics_metrics.description: Burial-society notices spell out entrance fee, weekly contributions, time to become 'free' (e.g., 'Members to be free in six months'), where to pay, and precisely what funeral goods/services are included (coffin materials and fittings, pall, porters, number of cloaks/hoods/gloves, burial fees paid if not exceeding a stated sum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about membership costs and what the contributions cover; itemise the coffin/attire and funeral personnel provided and state monetary limits or exclusions for burial fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pompous, Latinate, or polysyllabic diction as an advertising style device.
rubrics_metrics.description: Some adverts employ extravagant vocabulary and learned-sounding words (e.g., 'compendiosity', 'diaphaneity', 'pellucidity', 'jucundity') to amuse or impress readers, sometimes valuing sound over sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt florid language to charm or satirise certain audiences, but be aware it may prioritize sound/artifice over clarity and can signal pretension or humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of verse and rhyme in announcements and auction bills.
rubrics_metrics.description: Auctioneers and sellers sometimes frame notices in short poems or rhyming couplets (example: William Hall's auction verses) to make them memorable and attract attendances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose short, catchy verses to advertise sales or events; rhythm and humour can increase circulation and recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasise cheapness/economy and moral/patriotic benefits of low price.
rubrics_metrics.description: Ads stress low price as a virtue with larger social or national benefits (example: Romanis 'FOR STOCKINGS ... sixpence in a pair is worth saving' and the copy linking economy to national advantage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame low price as economically sensible and socially virtuous; connect thrift to broader benefits to persuade price-sensitive buyers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign/continental provenance and Parisian manufacture claims to signal fashion/exoticism.
rubrics_metrics.description: Merchants advertise 'Manufacturers from Paris' or 'from Paris, Manufacturers' and list fashionable goods (fans, ribbons, jewellery) to suggest continental style and authority; sometimes the foreign phrasing is imperfect but nonetheless used as a signal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke continental origin or fashionable foreign manufacture to claim trendiness; be careful with translation or grammar to avoid undermining credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posting bills and tickets over doors as an established distribution practice.
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices and tickets (e.g., apartments to let) were posted over doors and in public places as a common means of distribution from at least the 17th century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prominent public posting places to reach passersby; include succinct essential information since notices are seen briefly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of museum/exhibition framing and royal/noble visits to raise status.
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibitions and machines are framed as museum-like attractions whose visits by princesses, nobles, or royals (as in the Beetham story) are reported to elevate the inventor's reputation and spread fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicise visits or patronage by high-status figures and present the site as a public exhibition to attract wider audiences and lend prestige.
